input.instructions: Create a compact, accurate blueprint for an 8-to-12-minute educational lesson with exactly ten sequential teaching beats. Do not write full narration. Create exactly three measurable learning objectives. For every beat, provide one distinct complete factual claim, a concrete example, a concise editable visual direction, and one or two exact supplied source IDs. End the claim, example, and visual direction with complete punctuation. Every cited source excerpt must directly support the claim; reuse at least two important technical terms from each cited excerpt so support can be checked locally. Do not invent course assignments, policies, measurements, datasets, instruction encodings, or product behavior that is absent from the supplied excerpts. Keep the claim, example, and visual direction compact; a deterministic local expander will produce the full narration. Sequence the beats from foundations through application and end with a practical analysis checklist. Use only the supplied source excerpts for factual claims. Every factual claim must cite one or more supplied source IDs. Narration must describe information that is essential to understand visuals. Do not imitate a named creator or invent sources.
input.prompt:
Topic: CSCI-599: Computer Science Undergraduate Independent Study. This catalog entry has student-, instructor-, or term-specific content. Create a rigorous orientation companion that teaches the stable process, standards, planning methods, evaluation criteria, and representative examples without inventing a fixed RIT syllabus. Official catalog description: Students work with a supervising faculty member on topics of mutual interest. A student works with a potential faculty sponsor to draft a proposal that describes what a student plans to do, what deliverables are expected, how the student's work will be evaluated, and how much credit will be assigned for successful completion of the work. The faculty sponsor proposes the grade, but before the grade is officially recorded, the student must submit a final report that summarizes what was actually accomplished. Enrollment in this course requires permission from the department offering the course. Typically Offered: Fall, Spring, Summer Computing Intra-College Studies (CINT) CINT-91 The Entrepreneurial Mindset (0 Credits) Entrepreneurial activities drive the new economy. This course is open to all STEM students, as it is likely that they will be involved in entrepreneurial activities at some time in their careers. This might be when they have identified a compelling idea, it might be when a colleague starts a business and needs their expertise for the founding team, or it could be the result of an economic shift. The course discusses what it takes to be a successful entrepreneur or a member of a founding entrepreneurial team. It looks at the different contributions of technology, risk-taking, customer interactions, management, and fundraising. Contact Hours: Lecture 1.5 Typically Offered: Fall, Spring

Source excerpts:

[acm-code-of-ethics]
The ACM Code directs computing professionals to contribute to society and human well-being. Computing professionals should avoid harm. They should be honest and trustworthy. They should be fair and take action not to discriminate. They should respect the work required to produce new ideas and creative works. They should respect privacy. They should honor confidentiality. Professionals should strive to achieve high quality in both processes and products. They should maintain high standards of professional competence, conduct, and ethical practice. Robust security should be designed and implemented when appropriate. Ethical computing decisions identify stakeholders, foreseeable benefits and harms, uncertainty, alternatives, and obligations.

[acm-research-practice]
Responsible technical communication distinguishes claims from evidence. It cites prior work and identifies the contribution being reported. Methods should be described well enough for readers to evaluate the work. Results should be reported accurately rather than selected to create a misleading conclusion. Limitations and threats to validity should be made visible. Authors should preserve research integrity and avoid plagiarism, fabrication, and falsification. Conflicts and relevant relationships should be disclosed according to publication policy. A research project narrows a question, reviews literature, defines a reproducible method, evaluates results, and communicates for the intended audience.

Students work with a supervising faculty member on topics of mutual interest. A student works with a potential faculty sponsor to draft a proposal that describes what a student plans to do, what deliverables are expected, how the student's work will be evaluated, and how much credit will be assigned for successful completion of the work. The faculty sponsor proposes the grade, but before the grade is officially recorded, the student must submit a final report that summarizes what was actually accomplished. Enrollment in this course requires permission from the department offering the course. This course is open to all STEM students, as it is likely that they will be involved in entrepreneurial activities at some time in their careers. This might be when they have identified a compelling idea, it might be when a colleague starts a business and needs their expertise for the founding team, or it could be the result of an economic shift. The course discusses what it takes to be a successful entrepreneur or a member of a founding entrepreneurial team. It looks at the different contributions of technology, risk-taking, customer interactions, management, and fundraising. Contact Hours: Lecture 1.5 Typically Offered: Fall, Spring

beats.claim: CSCI-599 enables students to conduct independent research or entrepreneurial projects under faculty supervision.
beats.example: A student might develop a novel algorithm for data compression or design a prototype for a student-led tech startup.
beats.title: Course Purpose and Scope
beats.visualDirection: Display a simple flowchart showing 'Student Idea' -> 'Faculty Sponsor' -> 'Independent Study' with arrows indicating mutual interest.

beats.claim: Students must draft a proposal that outlines planned activities, expected deliverables, evaluation methods, and credit allocation.
beats.example: The proposal specifies a three-month timeline, a working prototype as the deliverable, peer review as evaluation, and 3 credits for completion.
beats.title: Proposal Drafting Process
beats.visualDirection: Show a template screenshot with labeled fields: 'Project Description', 'Deliverables', 'Evaluation Criteria', 'Credit Assignment'.

beats.claim: A potential faculty sponsor collaborates with the student to review and approve the proposal before work begins.
beats.example: The sponsor provides technical feedback on the methodology and confirms that the project aligns with departmental resources.
beats.title: Faculty Sponsor Role
beats.visualDirection: Illustrate a handshake icon between 'Student' and 'Faculty Sponsor' with a checklist labeled 'Proposal Review'.

beats.claim: The faculty sponsor proposes the final grade based on the completed work, but this grade is not officially recorded until the final report is submitted.
beats.example: The sponsor recommends a B+ after reviewing the final deliverables, but the grade remains pending until the student submits the final report.
beats.title: Grade Proposal Procedure
beats.visualDirection: Display a timeline with two nodes: 'Grade Proposed' and 'Grade Officially Recorded', connected by an arrow labeled 'Final Report Submission'.

beats.claim: Students must submit a final report that summarizes actual accomplishments before the grade is officially recorded.
beats.example: The report includes a summary of tasks completed, challenges encountered, and evidence of deliverables meeting the proposed criteria.
beats.title: Final Report Requirement
beats.visualDirection: Show a document icon with a checklist: 'Summary of Accomplishments', 'Deliverables Verification', 'Reflection on Process'.

beats.claim: Enrollment in CSCI-599 requires prior permission from the department offering the course.
beats.example: The student submits a formal request to the CS department chair, who approves the enrollment based on academic standing and project feasibility.
beats.title: Departmental Permission Requirement
beats.visualDirection: Display a stamp graphic labeled 'Departmental Permission Granted' next to a course registration form.

beats.claim: Students must adhere to professional ethics, including honesty, fairness, respect for privacy, and avoidance of harm in their research or entrepreneurial work.
beats.example: When developing a student tracking app, the student ensures data is anonymized and obtains informed consent from participants.
beats.title: Ethical Standards in Independent Study
beats.visualDirection: Show a shield icon with three sub-icons: 'Honesty', 'Privacy', 'Fairness', with a label 'Professional Ethics' above them.

beats.claim: Independent projects require responsible technical communication, including accurate reporting of results, clear citation of prior work, and disclosure of limitations.
beats.example: The student's final report cites three relevant papers, reports test results without selective editing, and lists data collection constraints.
beats.title: Research Integrity and Communication
beats.visualDirection: Display a document with callouts: 'Cite Prior Work', 'Report Results Accurately', 'Disclose Limitations'.

beats.claim: CSCI-599 supports both technical research and entrepreneurial activities, covering technology contributions, risk management, and team coordination.
beats.example: A student launching a coding bootcamp applies the course framework to outline curriculum design, fundraising needs, and risk mitigation strategies.
beats.title: Application to Entrepreneurial or Technical Projects
beats.visualDirection: Show a split graphic: left side 'Technical Research' with a code bracket, right side 'Entrepreneurial Project' with a lightbulb and handshake.

beats.claim: Students should verify that their project meets all course requirements before submission by checking proposal completeness, ethical compliance, and evaluation alignment.
beats.example: The checklist confirms: proposal drafted, sponsor approved, deliverables defined, ethics reviewed, final report ready, and departmental permission secured.
beats.title: Practical Analysis Checklist
beats.visualDirection: Display a printable checklist with checkboxes for: 'Proposal Approved', 'Ethics Reviewed', 'Deliverables Defined', 'Final Report Ready', 'Permission Secured'.

learningObjectives: Define the core components of a CSCI-599 proposal, including scope, deliverables, evaluation criteria, and credit allocation.
Explain the sequential workflow from proposal drafting to final report submission and grade proposal.
Identify the ethical and professional standards required for independent research and entrepreneurial or technical projects.
